kernelIdea: Add componentwise; multiply by expanding and using i² = −1, giving (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i; invert by multiplying by the conjugate over itself. ℂ is a field.

kernels.l1: Do one instruction, then the other. That is how you add them.
kernels.l2: To add two complex numbers, add the across parts and add the up parts. It is just doing one move and then the other.
kernels.l3: Complex numbers add piece by piece: across with across, up with up. To multiply, expand the brackets as usual and then replace i × i with −1.
kernels.l4: Add complex numbers by adding the parts separately. Multiply them by expanding the brackets and replacing i times i with −1. Every nonzero one can be divided by, so all four operations work.
kernels.l5: Complex arithmetic is real arithmetic in two components with one extra rule, i² = −1. Dividing works by clearing the bottom of the fraction, which module 5.4 explains properly.
kernels.l6: The complex numbers obey every arithmetic rule the reals do. Dividing works by clearing the bottom of the fraction — the trick module 5.4 names — and checking that it is never zero is the one thing that needs an argument.
kernels.l7: Addition works coordinate by coordinate; multiplication expands the brackets and uses that the turn unit squares to −1; division clears the bottom of the fraction, which module 5.4 explains. Every arithmetic rule of §4.1 survives.
kernels.l8: ℂ is a field because ℝ[x]/(x²+1) is a quotient by a maximal ideal; the inversion formula is the standard rationalisation in a quadratic extension.

kernel: Add componentwise; multiply by FOIL with i² = −1, giving (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i; invert by multiplying by the conjugate over itself; divide as z · (1/w). ℂ is a field.
objectives: Add, multiply, invert, and divide complex numbers
State that ℂ is a field
